section.title: Turn a personal constraint into a product brief
section.deck: Ryan Peterman describes how discomfort and dissatisfaction with existing keyboards shaped a hardware prototype.

blocks.text: Peterman traces the project to wrist pain that began while playing tennis and worsened during his work as a software engineer. He says ergonomic keyboards helped him, but many designs required a layout change he did not want to make while still using a laptop in meetings. Price also mattered. These are his own experiences, rather than general medical conclusions about a particular keyboard.
blocks.heading: Start with the actual constraint

blocks.text: The keyboard he settled on offered two features he valued: separate halves reduced an uncomfortable wrist angle, and tenting helped him keep his wrists in a more neutral position. But the product also left him with a specific list of frustrations: unused space, a wire connecting otherwise wireless halves, a plastic construction, and bulky tenting accessories. He cites a $100 keyboard and an additional $40 for plastic tenting legs as prices in his experience at the time.
blocks.heading: Convert complaints into requirements

blocks.text: The proposed alternative combined a minimal shape, fully wireless halves, an aluminum body, and familiar key positions. A compact tenting mechanism also served as a portable case. Peterman says manufacturing partners had produced a working prototype demonstrating feasibility. Fundraising and manufacturing were the next steps he described; the clip does not establish that the product had already shipped.
